blocks.x: A **programming language** is a set of words and rules used to give instructions to a computer. C++ is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world.
C++ began at Bell Labs in 1979. Bjarne Stroustrup built it as an extension of the older C language, and it has grown into a full language of its own.
Every C++ program has the same basic skeleton. Here is the general pattern.
`#include <iostream>` loads the library that lets your program write output. `int main()` is the **main function**, the place where every program starts running.
The braces `{` and `}` hold the statements that belong to `main`. `return 0;` ends the program and tells the computer it finished successfully.
`std::cout` is the **standard output stream**, the channel that carries text from your program to the screen. The `<<` symbol is the **insertion operator**, and it inserts a value into that stream.
This program prints `Hello, world!` on the screen. The `\n` inside the string is a **newline**, and it moves the cursor to the next line.

items: `std::cout` is the stream that sends text to the screen.
`<<` inserts a value into the stream.
`\n` moves output to a new line.
`return 0;` ends `main` and signals success.

blocks.x: You can print several lines by using `std::cout` more than once. Each statement runs in order, from top to bottom.
A common beginner mistake is forgetting the semicolon. Every statement in C++ must end with a `;`.
Now you are ready for the challenge. Use `std::cout` and `<<` to print the exact text it asks for.
In C++, you can create a variable at the exact spot where you first need it. You do not have to move every declaration to the top of the program.
This also works inside loops. A **for loop** is a statement that repeats a block of code a fixed number of times.
The loop can carry its own **counter**, a variable that tracks which round you are on. You declare it right in the loop header.
The header has three parts. `int counter = start` creates the counter, `counter < stop` decides when to stop, and `counter++` adds 1 after each round.
The counter `n` starts at 7. Each round prints `n`, then adds 1, and the loop stops before `n` reaches 10.

items: To **declare** a variable means to create it with a type and a name, like `int n`.
The **scope** of a variable is the region of code where that variable exists.
`n++` is short for `n = n + 1`.

blocks.x: A counter declared in the header belongs to the loop. When the loop ends, the counter is gone and its name cannot be used anymore.
Here `doubled` is declared inside the loop body. A fresh one is created on every round.
A common mistake is using the counter after the loop ends. Writing `std::cout << n;` below the loop causes an error, because `n` no longer exists there.
Now try the challenge. Declare your counter in the loop header and print one number per line.
A **bool** is a type that can hold only two values: `true` or `false`. The older C language had no true or false type, so C++ added `bool`.
Programs answer yes or no questions all the time. A `bool` stores that kind of answer.
bool variable_name = value;
`bool` is the type of the variable. `variable_name` is the name you choose, and `value` is `true`, `false`, or a comparison.

bool isSunny = true;
std::cout << isSunny;  // prints: 1
The variable `isSunny` stores the value `true`. By default `std::cout` prints `1` for `true` and `0` for `false`.
A **relational operator** compares two values. The `<` operator checks if the left value is less than the right value, and the answer is a `bool`.

bool result = (10 < 20);
std::cout << result;  // prints: 1
The comparison `10 < 20` is true, so `result` holds `true`. It still prints as `1` because we did not change the output style.

items: `bool` is the type for true or false values.
`true` and `false` are the only two bool literals.
**std::boolalpha** is a setting that tells `std::cout` to print bool values as words instead of numbers.

blocks.x:
bool check = (8 > 20);
std::cout << std::boolalpha << check;  // prints: false
The comparison `8 > 20` is false, so `check` holds `false`. With `std::boolalpha`, the output is the word `false` instead of `0`.
A common mistake is typing `True` or `False` with a capital letter. C++ only accepts the lowercase `true` and `false`.
In the challenge you will compare two numbers and print the result. Remember `std::boolalpha` so the answer prints as a word.
A **struct** is a group of related variables bundled together under one name. Programs use structs to keep connected data in one place, and structs are the first step toward classes.

In C++, the name of a struct is called its **tag**, and the tag becomes a real type name. You declare a variable as `MyType v;` without repeating `struct`, while older C code must write `struct MyType v;`.
`struct_name` is the tag you choose, and the braces hold the fields. The last line declares a variable of your new type.
`rex` is a variable of type `Dog`. Each variable inside a struct is called a **field**, and the **dot operator** `.` reaches one field, so `rex.age` means the `age` inside `rex`.

items: `struct` is the keyword that starts the definition.
The tag, like `Dog`, becomes a new type name.
A field is one variable inside, like `age`.
The dot `.` reaches a field, as in `rex.age`.

blocks.x: `std::cin` can fill a field directly. Put the field after `>>` just like any other variable.
A common mistake is forgetting the semicolon after the closing brace of a struct definition. If the compiler complains, check that spot first.
Now you are ready for the challenge.
So far you have printed text on a single line. Often a program needs one `std::cout` statement to print text across several lines.

An **escape sequence** is a short code inside a string that starts with a backslash `\` and stands for something you cannot type directly. The most common escape sequence is `\n`, which means start a new line.
std::cout << "first_part\nsecond_part\n";
The `\n` can sit anywhere inside the quotes. It is never printed as two characters, it just ends the current line and moves the output down.
This one statement printed three lines. Each `\n` ended the line it was on, so every word got its own line.
Two `\n` codes in a row make a blank line. The first one ends the current line, and the second one ends an empty line.

items: `\n` starts a new line.
`\t` inserts a tab, which is a wide space.
`\"` prints a double quote inside a string.
`\\` prints a single backslash.

blocks.x:
std::cout << "she said \"hi\"\n";
// she said "hi"
A common mistake is typing `/n` with a forward slash. Escape sequences only work with the backslash `\`, and `/n` prints as plain text.
Now use `\n` to print several lines, including a blank line, all from one single output statement.
So far your programs only printed values written inside the code. Most real programs need numbers from the person running them.
Data a program receives while it runs is called **input**. In C++ you read input with `std::cin`.

variable_type variable_name;
std::cin >> variable_name;
The first line declares a variable to hold the value. The `>>` operator takes what the user types and stores it in that variable.
When the program reaches `std::cin`, it pauses and waits. The user types a number, presses Enter, and the value lands in `score`.
To keep a result for later, use **assignment**: the `=` sign stores a value in a variable. You can also chain `<<` to print text and a value in one statement.

items: Declare two `int` variables, one for each number.
Read both numbers with `std::cin` and `>>`.
Add them and store the result with `=`.
Print a label and the result with chained `<<`.

blocks.x: The chained `std::cout` prints the text, then the value of `total`, then a newline. One statement does all three steps.

std::cin >> first >> second;      // reads two values at once
std::cout << total * 2 << "\n";   // math can go inside output
A common mistake is using `<<` with `std::cin`. Input flows into the variable, so `std::cin` always needs `>>`.
Now you are ready: read two integers from the user and print their total with a label.
In C++, dividing two integers always gives an integer. Any fractional part is simply dropped.
Dropping the fractional part is called **truncation**. The **modulus operator** `%` is a second division tool that gives you only the remainder.

int whole = dividend / divisor;
int left = dividend % divisor;
The `/` operator divides and throws the remainder away. The `%` operator divides and keeps only the remainder.
Nine goes into twenty six two times, with eight left over. So `/` gave `2` and `%` gave `8`.
When several operators appear in one expression, C++ follows a fixed order called **operator precedence**.

items: Parentheses `( )` are evaluated first.
Then `*`, `/`, and `%`, working left to right.
Then `+` and `-`, working left to right.

blocks.x:
int result = 10 + 6 * 9;
std::cout << result << "\n";  // 64
The `*` ran first, so `6 * 9` became `54`, and then `10 + 54` gave `64`. Add parentheses if you want the addition to happen first.

int forced = (10 + 6) * 9;
std::cout << forced << "\n";  // 144
A common beginner mistake is expecting a decimal answer. `19 / 2` gives `9`, not `9.5`, because both values are integers.
In the challenge, you will read two integers with `std::cin` and print their quotient and remainder.
Programs often need to compare two values, like a score against a passing mark. A **relational operator** compares two values and answers a yes-or-no question about them.
The answer has type `bool`, so it is always `true` or `false`. An `if` can test that answer and decide what runs.

if (left_value operator right_value)
    statement
Each value is one side of the comparison. The operator between them picks the question, and the whole expression becomes `true` or `false`.
The expression inside the parentheses is called the **condition**. Here `speed > limit` is `true`, so the message prints, and when a condition is `false` the statement is skipped.

items: `==` is `true` when both sides are equal.
`!=` is `true` when the two sides are different.
`<` and `>` check less than and greater than.
`<=` and `>=` are `true` even when the sides are equal.

blocks.x: Each `if` is checked on its own. Several relationships can be `true` at the same time, so several lines can print.
Both conditions are `true` here, so both messages print. Because your code has `using std::cout;`, you can write `cout` without the `std::` prefix.
A common mistake is typing `=` instead of `==`. `=` assigns a value, but `==` compares two values.
Now you are ready to read two integers and print every relationship that holds between them.
Programs often need to choose between two paths. This choosing is called **selection**.
The `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `true`. The `else` part runs when the condition is `false`.
A **condition** is an expression that gives a `bool` value, like `age > 12`.
The `condition` goes in parentheses. The line after `if` runs when it is `true`, and the line after `else` runs when it is `false`.
Here `age > 12` is `true`, so the first `cout` runs. The `else` part is skipped.

items: `if` starts the selection and holds the condition.
`else` covers every case where the condition is `false`.
Only one of the two paths ever runs.

blocks.x: You can also leave out `else` when there is nothing to do in the false case.
A common mistake is writing `=` instead of `==` in the condition. `=` changes the variable, while `==` compares.
Now try the challenge: read a number and choose which message to print.
Sometimes a program needs more than two paths. An **else if** chain lets you test several conditions in a row, one after another.
The computer checks each condition from top to bottom. As soon as one is `true`, its statement runs and the rest are skipped.
`condition1` is tested first. If it is `false`, `condition2` is tested. The final `else` runs only when every condition above it was `false`.
Here `temp >= 30` is `false`, so that line is skipped. Then `temp >= 20` is `true`, so `warm` prints and the chain ends.
Notice that `25` is also greater than `10`. That branch never runs because an earlier condition already matched.

items: Write the tests from the highest value down to the lowest.
Only the first `true` condition runs; the rest are skipped.
The final `else` is the catch-all case when nothing matched.
You can add as many `else if` parts as you need.

blocks.x: A common mistake is testing from lowest to highest. If `speed > 40` came first, it would match `70` too, and `too fast` could never print.
Another common mistake is using separate `if` statements instead of `else if`. Then several conditions can all be `true` and print more than one line.
Now try the challenge. Read a number with `cin` and use an `else if` chain, ordered from highest to lowest, to print the right message.
A **loop** is a statement that repeats a block of code. Programs use loops to do the same task many times without writing the same code many times.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. When the condition becomes `false`, the loop stops and the program moves on.
**Counter-controlled repetition** runs a loop an exact number of times. It uses a **counter**, which is a variable that counts how many times the loop has run.
In this pattern, `limit` stands for how many rounds you want. The condition `counter <= limit` is tested before each round, and `counter = counter + 1;` adds one after each round.
This prints the numbers 1 through 5, each on its own line. After the fifth round, `count` becomes 6, the condition is `false`, and the loop ends.

items: Initialization: set the counter before the loop, as in `int count = 1;`
Condition: test the counter before each round, as in `count <= 5`
Increment: add one to the counter after each round, as in `count = count + 1;`

blocks.x: A loop can also build up a running total. Start a variable at 0, then add each new value to it inside the loop.
Each round reads one value into `score` and adds it to `sum`. Integer division then truncates, so `sum / 3` drops any remainder.
A common mistake is forgetting to update the counter inside the loop. A loop whose condition never becomes `false` is an **infinite loop**, and it runs forever.
In the challenge, you will use a counter to read a fixed number of grades, add them to a total, and print the average.
Sometimes a program cannot know ahead of time how many values it will read. A counter-controlled loop needs a fixed count, so it cannot handle this case.
A **sentinel** is a special value that means the input is over. The loop repeats until the user types the sentinel, and the sentinel itself is never processed.

The first `cin >> value;` runs once before the loop, so the condition has something to test. The matching read at the bottom gets the next value, and the loop ends when that value equals the sentinel.
Here `0` is the sentinel. If the user types 5, then 7, then 0, the program prints 12.
To average the values, keep the running total in a **`double`**, a type that holds numbers with decimal places. Then the division keeps its fraction instead of truncating like integer division.
`fixed` and `setprecision` come from the `<iomanip>` header. Together they print the `double` with exactly two digits after the decimal point.

items: Read the first value before the loop starts.
Test that value in the `while` condition.
Process the value inside the body.
Read the next value as the last line of the body.

blocks.x: If the very first value typed is the sentinel, the body runs zero times. Your program should be ready for that empty case.
A common mistake is leaving out the second `cin >>` inside the body. The value never changes, so the loop runs forever.
In the challenge you will read values until the sentinel, then print the average with two decimals or a message when nothing was entered.
A **nested control structure** is one control statement placed inside another. In this lesson an `if`/`else` sits inside a `while` loop.
Programs need this when every repetition also requires a decision. The loop handles the repetition, and the `if` handles the choice for each value.
The `while` line controls how many times the body runs. The `if`/`else` inside makes one decision per trip, and each branch updates a different counter.
Each trip reads one answer, then the nested `if` adds `1` to exactly one counter. After six trips the condition `counter <= 6` becomes false and the totals print.

items: Initialize both counters to `0` before the loop starts.
Read one value per trip with `cin >> answer;`.
Let the nested `if`/`else` add `1` to exactly one counter.
Print the totals after the loop ends, not inside it.

blocks.x: Indentation shows what is inside what. The whole `if`/`else` belongs to the loop body, so the decision happens again on every single trip.
A common mistake is writing `++counter;` inside the `if` instead of the loop body. Then the counter grows only sometimes, and the loop may never end.
Now you are ready for the challenge: count each kind of exam result, print both totals, and add one extra message when the pass count is high.
A **reference parameter** is a function parameter that acts as another name for the caller's variable. A normal parameter receives a copy, so changes inside the function never reach the caller.

A function can return only one value. Reference parameters let it hand back extra results, so a common pattern is to return a `bool` for success and deliver data through a reference, like `bool deleteFirst(KEY_VALUE &kv);`.
The `&` after the type makes `parameter_name` a reference. Inside the function, using that name uses the caller's variable directly.
`num` is another name for `score` during the call. Assigning to `num` changes `score`, so the program prints -12.

items: **Pass by value**: the parameter is a copy, as in `void f(int x)`, so changes stay inside the function.
**Pass by reference**: the parameter is an alias, as in `void f(int &x)`, so changes reach the caller.
**Status return**: a `bool` return reports success while a reference carries the result.

blocks.x: `lastDigit` returns `false` for a negative input and leaves `digit` alone. Otherwise it stores the last digit in `digit` and returns `true`, and your homework uses this same idea to delete an item and hand its key back.
A common mistake is forgetting the `&`. Without it the function changes a private copy and the caller's variable never changes.
Now write the function for the challenge: test the input, store through the reference only on success, and return the matching `bool`.
Every array you have used so far had its size fixed in the code. A **dynamic array** is an array whose size is chosen while the program is running.
This matters when you cannot know the size ahead of time, like when the user types how many values there are. C++ creates such arrays with `new` and releases them with `delete[]`.

The result of `new` is stored in a **pointer**, a variable that holds the location of a value in memory. `new type[size]` reserves room for `size` values, and you use the pointer with `[ ]` exactly like a normal array name.
The program asks for exactly `count` integers, so no space is wasted. The last line returns that block of memory to the system.

items: `new type[size]` allocates an array during the run and returns a pointer to its first element.
`delete[] ptr` frees a whole array that came from `new type[size]`.
`delete ptr` without brackets frees one single value, so it must not be used on arrays.

blocks.x: A `for` loop is the usual way to fill a dynamic array, with the counter starting at `0` and stopping before the size. Your list assignment uses this same idea: it allocates storage with `new` and frees it with `delete[]` when the list is destroyed.
A common mistake is forgetting `delete[]`. Memory taken with `new` stays reserved until you free it, and forgetting is called a **memory leak**.
In the challenge you will read a size, allocate an array with `new`, fill it in a loop, print a total, and free it with `delete[]`.
A **capacity** is the total number of slots an array has. A **count** is how many of those slots currently hold real data.
Programs need both numbers because an array is usually bigger than the data inside it. Every list you build this semester tracks a `listCapacity` for the room and a `listCount` for the used slots.
The count starts at `0` and grows by one each time you store a value. The capacity is fixed when the array is created and never changes.
Here `capacity` holds the fixed size, `new int[capacity]` reserves that many slots, and `count` remembers how many are filled so far.
The value `42` went into slot `0`, and `count` rose to `1` while `capacity` stayed `10`.

items: `listCapacity`: the fixed number of slots, set once by `new`
`listCount`: how many slots hold real values right now
full: `count == capacity` means no room is left
empty: `count == 0` means nothing is stored yet

blocks.x: When reading input into an array, the loop must stop at the sentinel or when the array is full. Always test `count < capacity` before storing a new value.
Each trip through the loop stores one value at index `count` and then bumps `count`. The loop ends when the sentinel `0` appears or when every slot is used.
A common mistake is looping while `count <= capacity`, which writes one slot past the end. Valid indexes run from `0` to `capacity - 1`, so stop as soon as `count` equals `capacity`.
Your P1 list uses this same pair, `listCapacity` and `listCount`, to know where the next insert goes.
Now use count and capacity together to fill an array safely in the challenge.
A **class** bundles private data with the public functions allowed to touch it. It lets you build your own type, just like `int` or `bool`, but designed by you.
Programs model real things, like bank accounts and timers. A class keeps the data and its functions in one place, so outside code cannot put the data in a bad state.
A variable declared inside a class is a **member variable**. A function declared inside a class is a **member function**.

The `class` keyword starts the definition, and a semicolon must follow the closing brace. `public:` names what any code may call, `private:` names what only member functions may touch, and the function named like the class is the **constructor**, which runs when an object is created.
This only declares the class, it says what exists but not what the functions do. The function bodies are written outside the class, one by one.

The `::` symbol is the **scope resolution operator**, and `PiggyBank::total` means the `total` that belongs to `PiggyBank`. The `const` after the parameter list promises that the function will not change any member variable.

items: A **constructor** has no return type, and it sets starting values for the member variables.
`public:` members can be called from `main` or any other code.
`private:` members can be used only inside the class's own member functions.
An **object** is a variable whose type is a class.

blocks.x: Writing `PiggyBank bank;` creates an object and calls the constructor, so `cents` starts at 0. Each call to `deposit` changes `cents` through a member function, never directly.
A common mistake is touching private data from outside, like `bank.cents = 100;`. That is a compile error, because only member functions may use `cents`.
Your assignment uses this same idea: a class whose member functions are the only code allowed to change its data. Now finish the `Counter` class in the challenge.
A **constructor** is a special member function that runs automatically when an object is created. Its job is to give the object's data starting values.
A **default argument** is a value written next to a parameter, used when the caller passes nothing. With defaults, one constructor can serve callers who pass values and callers who pass none.
Without a constructor, member data holds garbage until someone sets it. Defaults make the safe choice the easy choice.
The constructor has the same name as the class and no return type. The `= default_value` part means the caller may skip that argument.
Object `a` got no argument, so `w` used the default `10`. Object `b` passed `25`, so the default was ignored.

items: The default is used only when the caller omits the argument, as in `Box a;`.
Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it must have one too.
Put the `= value` in the declaration inside the class, not again in an outside definition.

blocks.x: A constructor can take several defaults, like `Box(int w = 10, int h = 4)`. The caller fills arguments from left to right.

Box a;        // w is 10, h is 4
Box b(7);     // w is 7, h is 4
Box c(7, 9);  // w is 7, h is 9
A common mistake is writing `Box a();` to ask for the defaults. C++ treats that as a function declaration, so write `Box a;` with no parentheses.
Your list homework uses this idea so that `list myList;` builds a working list with no arguments. Now finish the `Tank` class in the challenge.
To **insert** a value at the front of an array means storing it at index 0. Every value already inside must move one slot to the right to make room.
Moving each value one slot over is called a **shift**. The shift must start at the last used slot and work toward the front, or data gets overwritten.
Your list ADT tracks `listCount` and `listCapacity`. After a successful insert, `listCount` grows by one, and P1's `insert` uses exactly this idea.
The loop starts `i` at `count`, which is the first empty slot. Each pass copies `data[i - 1]` into `data[i]`, and when the loop ends, slot 0 is free for `newValue`.
The 30 moved to slot 3, the 20 moved to slot 2, and the 10 moved to slot 1. Then 77 was stored at slot 0.

items: Make sure `count` is less than the capacity so there is room.
Loop `i` from `count` down to 1, copying `data[i - 1]` into `data[i]`.
Store the new value in `data[0]`.
Add one to `count`.

blocks.x: A common mistake is shifting forward, copying `data[i]` into `data[i + 1]` while `i` increases. That spreads the first value across the whole array and destroys the rest.
In the challenge you will read values into an array, shift them one slot right, place the new value at the front, and print the list.
Deleting the first entry of a list works like insert in reverse. Every other entry moves one slot toward the front, and the used count drops by one.
An array cannot hold a gap, so we close the gap by copying. A **shift left** means copying each entry into the slot just before it.
`deleteFirst(kv)` also saves the removed value into the reference parameter `kv` and returns a `bool`. If the list is empty, it returns `false` and does not touch `kv`.
`out = data[0];` saves the first entry before anything overwrites it. The loop copies each entry one slot left, and `count--;` marks the last slot as unused.
After the loop, the first three slots hold `20`, `30`, and `40`, and `count` is `3`. The old `40` still sits in slot 3, but `count` says it is no longer used.

items: the guard `if (listCount == 0) return false;` stops the function when there is nothing to delete
`kv = keyValues[0];` must happen before the shift, or the value is lost
the condition `i + 1 < listCount` keeps the loop from reading past the last used entry
`listCount--;` shrinks the used region by one

blocks.x: Notice the loop reads `data[i + 1]` and writes `data[i]`, the mirror of the insert shift. Your P1 homework uses this exact left shift inside `deleteFirst`.
A common mistake is writing the loop condition as `i < listCount`. That reads one slot past the last used entry and copies garbage into the list.
In the challenge you will read values into a list, delete the first one with this shift, and print what remains.
`insertAt(index, kv)` is a list function that places a new value at the position you pick. It returns `true` when the insert worked and `false` when it did not.
A **guard** is a check that rejects bad input before any data changes. For `insertAt`, the only legal positions are index 0 through `listCount` inclusive.
Inserting at index `listCount` is a legal **append**, which means adding right after the last used slot. Any index larger than `listCount` returns `false` and the list stays exactly as it was.
bool result = list_name.insertAt(position, new_value);
`position` is the index where the new value will sit, and `new_value` is what gets stored there. The returned `bool` tells you whether the guard accepted the position.

list scores(20);
scores.insertAt(0, 70);    // list: 70
scores.insertAt(1, 90);    // list: 70 90, an append
scores.insertAt(1, 80);    // list: 70 80 90
scores.insertAt(12, 50);   // returns false, no change
The call at index 1 pushed `90` one slot right to make room for `80`. The last call failed the guard because index 12 is beyond `listCount`, which was 3.

items: `index < listCount`: entries shift right one slot to open a gap.
`index == listCount`: a legal append, nothing needs to shift.
`index > listCount`: the guard rejects it and returns `false`.

blocks.x: When you shift by hand, loop from the back toward the front. Copying from the front first would overwrite a value before you save it.
A common mistake is writing the guard as `pos >= count`. That wrongly rejects the legal append, so the guard must be `pos > count`.
In the challenge you will read a list, an index, and a value, then apply this guard and shift yourself. Print `true` or `false`, then the list, to show what happened.
A **dynamic array** is an array created with `new`, with a size chosen while the program runs. Once created it cannot grow, so a full array is a real problem.
The **expand pattern** is the standard fix. You allocate a bigger array, copy the old values into it, delete the old array, and repoint your pointer at the new block.
Your list homework uses this inside a private `expand()` that runs when `listCount` reaches `listCapacity`. The four steps must happen in the right order.
`type` is the element type, `data` is the old pointer, and `count` is how many slots are used. `new_capacity` is the larger size you want.
After `delete[] data`, the variable `data` is a **dangling pointer**, a pointer that still holds an address whose memory was freed. The very next line repoints it, so it is never used while dangling.

items: Allocate: `new type[new_capacity]` reserves a fresh, larger block.
Copy: a `for` loop moves each used element into the new block.
Delete: `delete[] data` frees the old block.
Repoint: `data = bigger;` saves the new address in your pointer.

blocks.x: Order matters. If you call `delete[] data` before copying, the old values are gone, and if you repoint before deleting, you lose the old address and leak memory.
The guard `count == capacity` means you expand only when the array is truly full. Doubling with `capacity * 2` is common, but adding a fixed amount works too.
A common mistake is forgetting to update `capacity` after repointing. The program then still thinks the array is small, so it expands again too soon or writes past the new block.

Here is the one idea in this lesson: **a function can call itself.** Not by accident — on purpose, to hand off a smaller piece of its own job. That's called recursion. The first time you see it, it looks like it should run forever. It doesn't, and the easiest place to see why is a tree, because a tree is literally built out of smaller trees.
So forget code for a minute. We're going to look at a tiny tree, notice something obvious about it, and let that obvious thing write the function for us.

Start from your own class note: *“every node is a root of its own subtree.”* On a tree that's not a metaphor, it's literally true. Picture a node holding 10, with two kids: 6 on the left, 15 on the right. Now cover 10 with your thumb and just look at 6. All by itself, 6 is a complete little tree. Same with 15. So 10's whole job — “deal with my entire tree” — is really: deal with me, plus deal with two smaller trees that each have their own root.

Here's the lazy trick again, now on a tree. Somebody asks you: *add up every value in this tree.* Do the least work you possibly can. Take your own value. Ask your left subtree for its total. Ask your right subtree for its total. Add the three together and hand it back. You never walked the whole tree yourself — you added one number and made two phone calls.
In code. `tnode *t` is “the tree I was handed,” `t->val` is my own number, and `t->left` / `t->right` are the two smaller trees:

Read the last line as a plain sentence: “my value, plus whatever the left subtree adds up to, plus whatever the right subtree adds up to.” You put in your one number. The two `sumTree(...)` calls do all the rest. You are not walking the tree; you're delegating twice.

Now the first line — the stopper. In the numbers version the chain stopped at 0. On a tree it stops at an **empty tree**: a branch that points to `nullptr`. A tree with nothing in it adds up to 0, and it makes no phone calls. That's the base case. Leave it out and a call eventually does `nullptr->val`, and the program crashes. Every recursion needs a floor. For trees, the floor is always “the tree is empty.”
Watch it run on that little 10 / 6 / 15 tree. Down the calls go, then the empty trees answer 0, then the answers add up on the way back:

sumTree(10)
  = 10 + sumTree(6) + sumTree(15)

  sumTree(6)  = 6  + sumTree(null) + sumTree(null) = 6  + 0 + 0 = 6
  sumTree(15) = 15 + sumTree(null) + sumTree(null) = 15 + 0 + 0 = 15

  = 10 + 6 + 15 = 31

That's the whole leap from numbers to trees, and it's smaller than it looks. The numbers version made **one** phone call: `sumTo(n - 1)`. The tree version makes **two**: `sumTree(t->left)` and `sumTree(t->right)`. Everything else is identical — do your one bit, delegate the rest, keep a base case that stops the chain. One friend became two friends. Nothing else changed.

And your last note — *“must be true or becoming true.”* The promise here is: “give me a tree, I hand back the total of every value in it.” Each call keeps that promise as long as its two smaller calls keep theirs, and the empty tree keeps it for free. So don't try to hold the whole tree in your head at once — you can't, and you don't need to. Write your one step. Write the empty-tree base case. Trust the two calls. One more idea and you can read any tree function ever written. A recursive function has **two moments**: the code *before* the recursive call, and the code *after* it. Before-code runs on the way down. After-code runs on the way back up.

Picture it like a stack of paused people. When `climb(3)` reaches its recursive call, it *pauses mid-sentence* and waits. `climb(2)` starts, pauses. `climb(1)` starts, pauses. `climb(0)` hits the base case and does nothing. Now everyone un-pauses **in reverse order**, each finishing their sentence.

  climb(2)  pauses, waiting on climb(1)
    climb(1)  pauses, waiting on climb(0)

    climb(1)  resumes: prints 1
  climb(2)  resumes: prints 2

This lesson's whole job is the tiny parts: `*`, `->`, `new`, and `nullptr`. Tree code is nothing but those four, so let's get every one of them exactly right. One picture the whole way: **a node is a box with three slots, and a pointer is a slip of paper with a box's address on it** — or the word *none*.

That's the box. `val` holds a plain number. `left` and `right` don't hold boxes — they hold **slips**: the address of another box, or *none*. A box never contains another box. It only holds directions to one.

**`tnode *t`** — read the `*` as “slip of paper for.” So `t` is not a box. It's a slip. This is the single most common confusion in the whole chapter: when you see `tnode *`, think *slip*, never *box*.
**`nullptr`** — the slip that says *none*. There is no box at the other end. An empty tree is exactly this: one slip, reading none.
**`new tnode`** — go buy a fresh box. `new` hands you back its address, which you catch in a slip. Then you fill the slots one at a time:

tnode *root = new tnode;   // buy a box, keep the slip in root
root->val = r;             // slot 1: the number
root->left = nullptr;      // slot 2: none (no left child yet)
root->right = nullptr;     // slot 3: none

**`->`** — the arrow is the part most people quietly never learn, so here it is exactly: **follow the slip to its box, then open one slot.** `root->val` means *go to root's box, open the val slot.* (If it helps once: `root->val` is short for `(*root).val` — follow, then dot into the slot. Nobody writes the long form. The arrow *is* “follow, then open.”)

Now the key tiny fact. What's *in* `root->left`? A slip. The same kind of thing as `root` itself — both are `tnode *`. So attaching a child is just: buy a box, put its slip into the left slot, then follow that slip to fill the new box:

root->left = new tnode;        // buy a box, slip goes in root's left slot
root->left->val = a;           // follow root, follow left, open val
root->left->left = nullptr;    // the new box's own slots: none
root->left->right = nullptr;

Read `root->left->val` as three steps: follow `root` to its box, follow that box's `left` slip to the child box, open the child's `val`. Arrows chain. The right child is the same four lines with `right` in place of `left` — that's your challenge.
Checking a slip before following it. The challenge ends by asking whether the left child has a left child of its own. You don't open anything — you *look at the slip*:
if (root->left->left == nullptr) cout << "null\n";

Follow root, follow left, and just *read* the left slot: it says none. That's the whole test. **Never** write `root->left->left->val` here — that would try to open a box that doesn't exist, and the program crashes. Rule for life: `->` on a slip that says none is a crash. Test the slip *first*, and test the slip, not the contents.

Declaring versus using: the `*` in `tnode *t` only *declares* that `t` is a slip. The `->` *uses* the slip by following it. Two different jobs, so two different symbols. If you ever wonder “why `*` here but `->` there,” that's the answer.

`int` — promises to hand back a number. `tnode *t` — you're handed a slip. `t == nullptr` — does the slip say none? then the answer is 0 and you're done; nothing below runs on an empty slip. `t->val` — follow the slip, open my number. `sumTree(t->left)` — `t->left` is a slip too, so hand it to a fresh copy of the function; inside that copy, its `t` *is* the left child's slip. The `+` signs are plain addition. `return` sends the total back to whoever handed you your slip.

    A is a real box. val = 10.
    A's left slot: slip→B. Hand it over.

            B's right: none → sumTree(none) returns 0 at once

    A's right slot: none → sumTree(none) returns 0

**From the board: “must be true or becoming true.”** The BST property — smaller keys left, bigger keys right, at *every* node — is an **invariant**: a promise every operation is judged against. Insert keeps it true by choosing a side. Remove will keep it true by promoting the right replacement. Search *relies* on it to skip half the tree at each step. Whenever you're stuck on any tree function, ask one question: *what does the invariant force here?*

This is the most important lesson of the chapter, and it comes down to two ideas. Idea one: inserting into a tree is the same lazy delegation you already know. Idea two: the strange `tnode *&t` is what lets the new node actually *attach*. Take them one at a time.

**Idea one.** Standing at any node, you ask exactly one question: *is my new value smaller than this node's value?* Smaller means the value belongs somewhere in the left subtree, so you hand the ENTIRE job to the left child and you are done. Otherwise, hand it to the right child. You never look at the whole tree. One question, then delegate.

**Idea two.** Read `tnode *&t` as: *t is a nickname for the caller's actual pointer variable*. Not a copy of it. The variable itself. So when the call is `insert(root->left, v)`, the name `t` inside that call **is** `root->left`. Writing to `t` writes into that field of the parent node.

Now the base case makes sense. The walk ends when you get handed a pointer that is `nullptr`, meaning an empty slot in some parent. Because `t` *is* that slot, the single line `t = new tnode;` stores the new node's address **into the parent's left or right field**. That one assignment is the hook-up. No extra wiring, no returning pointers, nothing.
Trace inserting 8 into a tree whose root is 50 with a left child 30:

insert(root, 8)          // t is the variable root.  8 < 50, go left
  insert(root->left, 8)  // t IS root->left (the node 50's left field).  8 < 30, go left
    insert(root->left->left, 8)  // t IS node 30's left field, which is nullptr
      t = new tnode;     // node 30's left field now points at the new node
      t->val = 8;        // 8 is hooked into the tree. done.

The idea first, no code. In a BST, smaller things always live to the left. So the smallest thing of all is as far left as you can possibly go. Not the deepest node — the **leftmost** one. On the tree from class: start at 50. Go left to 25. Go left to 12. Go left to 8. 8 has no left child, so stop. The min is 8. Four steps, no thinking.

Now the interesting part: the line you crossed out. `if (p == 0) return 0;` — why did that get scratched? Because **0 might be a real key.** If the tree is empty and you hand back 0, the caller can't tell “empty” from “the min is zero.” That's a lie disguised as an answer. The board's loop dodges the problem by *requiring* a non-empty tree: whoever calls it must check first. That's a real design choice, and it's exactly why this lesson's version has a different shape.

This lesson's `findMin` returns a `bool` — *did I find one?* — and delivers the actual value through a reference, `int &m`. Empty tree: return false, leave `m` alone. And the lesson does it recursively — the same walk, delegated instead of looped:

Three sentences. “If there's no tree, say no.” “If I have no left child, I'm the answer — store me, say yes.” “Otherwise, ask my left subtree and pass along whatever it says.” That last line is the relay again: the leftmost call sets `m` and returns true, and every call above it hands that `true` straight up.

Loop or recursion — which is *right*? Both. They take the identical steps: the loop moves `p` down one node; recursion hands `t->left` to a fresh call. Every recursive tree operation needs a node pointer that changes with each call. But the user of your class only has a value, and should never touch `root`.
The solution is to split every operation into two functions. A **wrapper** is a public function that takes only the user's value.
A **recursive helper** is a private function that takes a node pointer plus the value. It does the real work, and the wrapper just starts it off.
`root` sits in the private section so only member functions can touch it. The helper is private because users should never pass a node pointer themselves.
When the user writes `tree.add(42);`, the wrapper hands `root` and `42` to `addRec`. The caller never sees a pointer.

items: The user calls a public function like `add(42)` with only a value.
The wrapper calls the helper, passing `root` as the starting pointer.
The helper recurses left or right until it reaches a `nullptr` spot.
The calls unwind, and the wrapper finishes.

Here is the one idea in this lesson: **a new class can start as a copy of an old one.** You don't rewrite anything. You say “build on that,” and you get all of it for free. Then you change the one thing you want to change.
In your notes, the old class is the BST. The new class is AVL, the balanced tree. Today is about the *hook-up* between them. No balancing yet, just how one class sits on top of another.

Start with something you already know: a class has drawers for its members. The only question is **who is allowed to open each drawer.** `public`: anyone. `private`: only the class itself. And the new one, `protected`: the class itself **and its children**. Nobody else. Think of it as “family only.”

Why does protected exist? Because the parent wants its kids to reach `root` and `nCount`, but does not want `main` reaching in. Private would lock out the kids. Public would let in everyone. Protected is exactly in between.
Now the child. One line makes it:

Read it as “agrove is a grove, plus more.” From this line on, agrove has a root, a count, every helper, `height()`, `balanced()` — all of it, without writing any of it. That's inheritance. That's the whole word.

Now the sentence your professor said last class: *“preparing for the other class to have its own insert.”* Here's what it means in plain words. Normally a child just uses the parent's insert as-is. But AVL needs **its own** insert, one that balances. For a child to be allowed to *replace* a function, the parent has to have said, in advance, “you may replace this one.” The way the parent says it is one word: **virtual**.

So `virtual bool insert(...)` in the base class means: *I'm writing this today knowing a class built on me will replace it later.* That's P4 planning for P5. Without that word, the door is locked and the child is stuck with the parent's insert forever.

It goes back to the parent's insert — `grove::insert(p)` means “grove's insert, not mine” — lets that do all the real work, and then does one extra thing after.

That is the entire design of AVL, written in your notes as `BST::insert(p); bal(p);`. Line one: return to the parent's insert. Line two: the only thing AVL actually adds. Everything you'll learn about balancing goes in line two. Line one never changes.

Last piece: why the word `virtual` matters so much. Look at `main`: `grove &T = G;`. Main holds your tree as a plain grove. It has no idea it's really an agrove. It calls `T.insert(p)` — and the **child's** insert runs anyway. That's what virtual buys. Without it, main would get the parent's insert, and the child's extra step would silently never happen: a balanced tree that never balances. Here is the one idea: **a balanced tree fixes itself by rotating.** When a node gets two levels heavier on one side, its heavy child steps up, the node steps down, and the subtree caught in the middle hops across. Nothing else in the tree notices. Done at every node on the way back up the recursion, this keeps the whole tree short — that's the entire reason AVL exists.

Start with one number per node: **balance = height(left) − height(right).** The sign tells you which way the node leans. Positive means the left side is winning the subtraction — *left heavy*. Negative means *right heavy*. Zero means even. An AVL tree promises that every node's balance stays at −1, 0, or +1. The moment one hits ±2, you rotate.

A heads-up if you watch YouTube on this: some videos count an empty tree as −1 (“underwater”) and a leaf as 0. **Your professor counts empty as 0 and a leaf as 1** — his correct output prints leaves at height 1. Same math, shifted by one; every balance comes out identical. Use his numbers in your code, because the grader prints them.
The sign also tells you what to do. Left heavy? Throw nodes to the right — a **right rotation**. Right heavy? Throw nodes to the left — a **left rotation**. That's the whole vocabulary.

Now the picture, and the one thing to hold onto: **only two nodes ever move. Everything else just follows.** Call the heavy node **x** and its heavy child **y**. Rotating means y steps up into x's spot and x steps down beside it. The three subtrees hanging off them don't get “computed” — they land where the invariant already says they must:

x                      y
       / \                    / \
      y   C       ---->      A   x
     / \                        / \
    A   B                      B   C

  A < y < B < x < C   before AND after.
  Only x and y swapped places. A, B, C kept their order.
  B is the one that "hops": it was y's right, now it's x's left.

Check the middle one, B, because that's the only subtree that changes parents. Before: bigger than y, smaller than x. After: bigger than y, smaller than x. Same sentence. Rotation moves *pointers*, never *order* — which is why it's allowed. That picture in code is four pointer moves, two height fixes, and one reassignment:

void agrove::rotateRight(tnode *&t1) {   // t1 is x, left heavy
    tnode *t2 = t1->left;                 // t2 is y
    t1->left = t2->right;                 // B hops over to x's left
    t2->right = t1;                       // x hangs under y
    t1->h = calcHeight(t1);               // x is lower now: fix it first
    t2->h = calcHeight(t2);               // then y, which sits on top of x
    t1 = t2;                              // the parent's pointer now holds y
}

Three places people slip. Save `t2` *before* you touch anything. Fix heights bottom-up: x first, then y, because y's height depends on x's. And the last line writes through the reference — `tnode *&` again — so the *parent's* pointer now holds y. `rotateLeft` is the mirror: swap every `left` and `right`.

Now the four dances, using the smallest possible trees. Insert **3, 2, 1**: 3 goes left heavy with balance +2, and the heavy child 2 leans the same way (its 1 is on the left). A straight line. One right rotation: 2 on top, 1 and 3 beside it. Done.

Insert **3, 1, 2**: 3 is left heavy again, +2. But look at the heavy child, 1 — its 2 is on its *right*. A kink. Try the plain right rotation anyway and watch it fail: 1 goes on top, 3 drops to the right, 2 has to go under 3 on the left… and now the 1 is right heavy by 2. You just moved the problem. So first straighten the kink: a *left* rotation on the child 1 turns 3 → 1 → 2 into the straight line 3 → 2 → 1. *Then* the right rotation on 3 works: 2 on top, 1 and 3 beside it. That's a **left-right** rotation. Two moves.

The right-heavy cases are the mirror image. Insert **1, 2, 3**: straight line, one left rotation. Insert **1, 3, 2**: kink — right rotation on the child 3 first, then left rotation on 1. That's **right-left**. Your class chain 100 → 200 → 150 is exactly this one.
